questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a continuing resolution does
questions.stem: A revision flashcard describes a short-term funding measure used when a new appropriation has not been enacted. Which statement describes it best?

options.text: It is a full year's appropriation enacted in advance of the new fiscal year
options.misconception: treats a continuing resolution as a full appropriation

options.text: It lets the President fund new programmes for the duration of the funding gap
options.misconception: believes a continuing resolution authorises new spending

options.text: It temporarily extends existing funding at the same rate and conditions
It permanently fixes federal spending levels until Congress acts again
options.misconception: assumes a continuing resolution lasts longer than one period

questions.explanation: A continuing resolution continues prior-year funding at the same rate and conditions for a short period, avoiding a shutdown. It authorises no new programmes and is not an annual appropriation.
questions.hint: Ask what it continues rather than what it creates.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why appropriated funds cannot be withheld
questions.stem: One member of the revision group asks whether the President may hold back money that Congress has already appropriated for a programme.

options.text: Yes, because the President may reduce spending to keep the deficit down
options.misconception: treats deficit control as a licence to withhold funds

options.text: No, because impoundment of appropriated funds is not permitted
Yes, but only if Congress has not yet made the appropriation
options.misconception: confuses enactment timing with available funds

options.text: No, because the President may suspend any programme at his discretion
options.misconception: invents a presidential suspension power that does not exist

questions.explanation: The President cannot hold back money Congress has appropriated, and any deferral or rescission must go through the congressional disapproval process. Deficit control licenses no withholding.
questions.hint: Ask whose approval the statute requires.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how automatic across-the-board cuts operate

stimulus.body: A study group's notes describe a statutory rule: if outlays in a later year exceed a legislated ceiling, automatic across-the-board cuts are made to non-exempt budget authority, and the President must carry them out. The notes add that the rule applies to discretionary accounts and not to mandatory benefit programmes.

questions.stem: According to the notes, what happens when the ceiling is reached?

options.text: Mandatory benefit programmes are cut first, because they make up the largest share
options.misconception: thinks mandatory programmes are the first target of cuts

options.text: Congress must pass a new statute before any of the cuts take effect
options.misconception: treats automatic cuts as requiring a fresh act

options.text: The President may choose which programmes to cut first
options.misconception: believes the President chooses how to apply the cuts

options.text: Across-the-board cuts are made automatically and the President must execute them

questions.explanation: Sequestration operates automatically once the ceiling is reached, taking effect without a new act. Mandatory programmes are exempt, which is why the rule covers discretionary accounts.
questions.hint: Ask whether a new law is needed to trigger the cuts.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The unified budget and off-budget items
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the unified budget requirement treats off-budget items
questions.stem: One student in the revision group asks how the requirement for a single budget affects programmes that were moved outside the ordinary budget process.

answer.exemplar: The constitutional requirement is that all federal money is presented and voted on in one budget, so programmes placed outside it by statute, such as certain trust funds, are exceptions created by Congress rather than a separate sovereign budget. A student should say that off-budget status comes from statute and still requires appropriations unless Congress provides otherwise.

questions.explanation: The unified budget requirement is constitutional, while off-budget trust fund status is statutory. It reflects a choice by Congress rather than a second sovereign budget.
questions.hint: Ask whether the exception comes from the text or a statute.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a yearly deficit from outlays and receipts
questions.stem: A revision flashcard shows a year with outlays of 1.4 trillion and revenues of 1.1 trillion and asks what the resulting deficit is.

options.text: It depends on interest on the debt, since interest is part of the deficit
options.misconception: confuses the deficit calculation with the debt total

options.text: The national debt must rise by 300 billion within the same year
options.misconception: treats an annual deficit as the total outstanding debt

options.text: Nothing, because the deficit is offset by future budget surpluses
options.misconception: assumes future surpluses cancel a deficit at once

options.text: 300 billion, because the deficit is that year's excess of spending over receipts

questions.explanation: The deficit is that year's outlays less its revenues, so the figure shown is 300 billion. The debt is the running total of past deficits net of surpluses, and interest enters the outlay side.
questions.hint: Ask what period the figure covers.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply an automatic offset requirement to a proposal

stimulus.body: A revision handout summarises a rule that requires any bill increasing mandatory spending or reducing revenue to be offset by an equal change elsewhere, unless Congress expressly waives the requirement. The handout notes that the budget office scores each bill and reports the offset amount.

questions.stem: Under the rule in the handout, what happens to a bill that adds a new mandatory benefit?

options.text: It must be reported by the budget office before it can be debated
options.misconception: treats a score as a procedural gate on debate

options.text: It becomes effective only if it clears the statutory budget ceiling
options.misconception: conflates an offset rule with the deficit ceiling

options.text: It must include an offsetting change unless Congress waives the requirement
It takes effect only if the offset appears in the following year's budget
options.misconception: assumes the offset may be deferred to a later year

questions.explanation: The rule requires new mandatory spending or reduced revenue to be offset unless Congress waives it; the budget office only reports the score. The offset must be in the same legislation, not deferred.
questions.hint: Ask whether the offset may wait for the next budget.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a baseline budget holds constant
questions.stem: The revision group studies a rule under which the cost of a proposal is measured against the level of spending that would continue under current law.

options.text: The baseline is the largest budget the President proposed in any year
options.misconception: confuses the baseline with a presidential budget proposal

options.text: The baseline projects current law spending forward without new policy
The baseline is the highest spending level of the previous decade
options.misconception: invents a historical-spending baseline that does not exist

options.text: The baseline is fixed by the deficit ceiling for the comparison year
options.misconception: ties the baseline to the ceiling rather than to current law

questions.explanation: A baseline projects current law forward and measures proposals against it, so a proposal can appear more expensive than it is. It is not a presidential proposal, a historical high, or the ceiling.
questions.hint: Ask what the baseline holds constant.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the budget office's role and its limits
questions.stem: A revision card asks two things: what the Congressional Budget Office does when it scores a bill, and what it cannot do.

options.text: It scores bills and drafts the replacement text that will be offered
options.misconception: confuses the office with the drafting committee

options.text: It scores bills and decides which version will be reported by a committee
options.misconception: makes the budget office the master of legislative procedure

options.text: It scores bills and provides budget information, but it neither drafts nor enacts bills
It scores bills and instructs committees on how they should vote
options.misconception: treats the budget office as directing members on voting

questions.explanation: The budget office scores bills and supplies budget information but neither drafts nor enacts legislation. Describing it as a text writer, a procedural master, or a vote director misstates its role.
questions.hint: Ask what the office is not allowed to do.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what happens when a continuing resolution expires
questions.stem: One note in the revision packet explains what happens when a continuing resolution expires without a replacement appropriation.

options.text: Funding continues at the prior rate, because expired resolutions keep operating
options.misconception: believes an expired resolution continues to operate

options.text: The President may extend the funding himself for a further period
options.misconception: invents unilateral presidential extension of appropriations

options.text: Agencies continue at reduced levels until Congress returns from recess
options.misconception: assumes reduced spending continues without authority

options.text: The affected funding lapses and the lapse of appropriations takes effect

questions.explanation: When a continuing resolution ends without a replacement appropriation, the funds it carried lapse and the consequences follow. There is no unilateral extension and no automatic reduced-level spending.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the money when the authority ends.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a deferral of appropriated funds needs Congress
questions.stem: A revision prompt asks the group to explain why a proposal to defer spending already appropriated cannot simply be announced by the executive branch.

answer.exemplar: Because appropriated funds may not be withheld by the executive, a proposed deferral or rescission must be transmitted to Congress and takes effect only if Congress does not disapprove it within the statutory window. The answer should identify the congressional approval mechanism rather than treating an executive announcement as self-executing.

questions.explanation: Withholding appropriated funds needs congressional approval under the impoundment process, so an announcement alone changes nothing. Executive discretion cannot replace that statutory step.
questions.hint: Ask whose approval the statute requires.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify which outlays are exempt from sequestration
questions.stem: One revision question asks which category of outlay is never reduced by an automatic sequestration.

options.text: Grants to state and local governments for transportation work
options.misconception: assumes grant programmes are shielded from automatic cuts

options.text: Pay for federal civilian personnel within the base budget
options.misconception: believes personnel costs are exempt from the cuts

options.text: Interest on the public debt owed to the public
Contract awards for new weapons systems and equipment
options.misconception: treats defence contract spending as exempt from the cuts

questions.explanation: Interest on the public debt is not reduced, because the obligation is already incurred, and mandatory programmes are protected. Discretionary grant, personnel, and contract accounts are within reach.
questions.hint: Ask which obligation is already fixed by prior law.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The unified budget and off-budget items
questions.learningObjective: Explain the legal effect of an off-budget label

stimulus.body: A revision worksheet lists three federal funds and marks two of them with a note reading off-budget by statute. The worksheet asks students to explain what the label does and does not mean for congressional power to spend from those funds.

questions.stem: According to the worksheet, what follows from the label?

options.text: Congress may spend from those funds without any appropriation at all
options.misconception: reads off-budget status as self-executing spending power

options.text: Congress still appropriates from them but they are displayed outside the main budget
The funds are governed by state law because the federal budget does not reach them
options.misconception: subjects federal trust funds to state law

options.text: Congress may spend from them only in years when the deficit ceiling is raised
options.misconception: ties off-budget funds to the ceiling mechanism

questions.explanation: Off-budget status is a statutory accounting arrangement: the funds are displayed separately but still require appropriations. It creates neither self-executing spending power nor a state-law regime.
questions.hint: Ask what still has to happen before money moves.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of raising the statutory debt limit
questions.stem: The revision group turns to the debt limit and asks what happens when the limit is raised.

options.text: Congress authorises additional borrowing to cover a projected shortfall in receipts
The government receives new revenue, because the limit is a revenue measure
options.misconception: treats a debt ceiling increase as new revenue

options.text: Spending is reduced automatically to bring the debt back under the limit
options.misconception: conflates the debt ceiling with the sequestration mechanism

options.text: The deficit for the year is cancelled, because borrowing eliminates the gap
options.misconception: believes borrowing erases the deficit

questions.explanation: Raising the debt limit authorises additional borrowing so payments can be made when receipts fall short. It supplies no revenue and cancels no deficit; automatic cuts are separate.
questions.hint: Ask what the limit governs: borrowing or revenue.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a failed offset is cured

stimulus.body: A handout states that when an automatic offset rule applies, the budget office must certify whether the legislation complies, and that a bill which fails to comply takes effect only if the House and the Senate each waive the requirement. The handout adds that a single house cannot waive it alone.

questions.stem: Under the rule described, what happens to a bill that does not comply?

options.text: It is sent back to the drafting committee for a new cost estimate
options.misconception: treats non-compliance as a procedural remand

options.text: It takes effect but is subject to an automatic cut if the ceiling is hit
options.misconception: links an offset failure to the sequestration mechanism

options.text: It is struck down as a violation of the rules of that chamber
options.misconception: invents a chamber rule invalidating such legislation

options.text: It takes effect only if both chambers waive the requirement

questions.explanation: Each chamber must waive the requirement separately, so one chamber acting alone is not enough. Non-compliance is not remedied by a remand, an automatic cut, or a procedural violation.
questions.hint: Ask how many chambers must act.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a proposal scores above its expected cost
questions.stem: A student asks why a proposal can score as costing more than its sponsors expect under a pay-as-you-go rule.

options.text: Because the baseline includes spending that the sponsors intend to cut
options.misconception: assumes the baseline is loaded with proposals

options.text: Because the baseline holds current spending constant and the proposal adds to it
Because the sponsors are scored against the highest year of the programme
options.misconception: uses the peak-year spending level as the baseline

options.text: Because proposals are always scored against the next year's appropriations
options.misconception: scores proposals against a future appropriations level

questions.explanation: A proposal looks costlier because the baseline holds current law spending in place, so new spending appears as an increase. The baseline is not built from sponsors' proposals or peak-year figures.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison line holds fixed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the budget office is insulated from political direction
questions.stem: Members of the revision group ask a student to explain why the Congressional Budget Office is not permitted to take direction from individual members of Congress on what to estimate.

answer.exemplar: The budget office answers to Congress as a whole and takes direction only through statutory instructions, so that its estimates can be relied on as impartial. A member may request information, but the office decides for itself what work to do, which is what keeps its scoring free of political instruction from either chamber or committee.

questions.explanation: Direction reaches the office only through statute, and members may request information but cannot instruct the work. This insulation is what keeps its scores usable in a partisan debate.
questions.hint: Ask through what channel the office is directed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the rate at which a continuing resolution operates
questions.stem: A revision flashcard notes that a continuing resolution usually continues appropriations at the rate in effect for the preceding period.

options.text: Funding continues at the prior rate and under the prior conditions
Funding continues at the rate the President requested in his budget
options.misconception: assumes the continuing resolution adopts the budget rate

options.text: Funding continues at a reduced rate fixed by the agency itself
options.misconception: lets individual agencies set the continuing rate

options.text: Funding continues at a rate set by whichever chamber acts first
options.misconception: invents chamber-by-chamber control of the rate

questions.explanation: A continuing resolution normally continues prior-year appropriations at the same rate and conditions, keeping programmes at their current level. It adopts neither the budget rate nor agency-set rates.
questions.hint: Ask whose numbers the continuing rate comes from.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify which executive proposals the disapproval process covers
questions.stem: A member of the revision group asks which of two executive proposals the congressional disapproval process covers.

options.text: A plan to spend an appropriation on a different programme
options.misconception: ignores that reprogramming is a different mechanism

options.text: A plan to hire additional staff at a federal office
options.misconception: treats hiring decisions as needing disapproval

options.text: A plan to cancel money Congress already appropriated
A plan to delay the start of a programme Congress authorised
options.misconception: confuses delayed new authority with rescission

questions.explanation: The disapproval process covers rescissions of appropriated funds and deferrals of money to be spent, so cancelling an appropriation falls within it. Reprogramming and delayed authority are separate.
questions.hint: Ask whether money already granted is involved.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the trigger and the actor in automatic cuts
questions.stem: Two questions come up in revision: what triggers automatic across-the-board cuts, and what happens once they are triggered.

options.text: They are triggered when a spending cap is breached, and Congress must then enact them
options.misconception: moves the trigger from the ceiling to a spending cap

options.text: They are triggered by the President's budget request, and he then sets the amounts
options.misconception: makes the budget request the trigger for automatic cuts

options.text: They are triggered by a statutory ceiling on borrowing, and Congress may waive them
options.misconception: conflates the debt ceiling with the sequestration trigger

options.text: They are triggered by reaching a statutory deficit ceiling, and the President must execute them

questions.explanation: The trigger is reaching the legislated ceiling on the deficit, and once met the cuts operate by statute, so the President must execute them. A spending cap or the debt ceiling each fail.
questions.hint: Ask what condition is met and who then acts.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The unified budget and off-budget items
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a statutory trust fund exception is treated

stimulus.body: A revision sheet describes a trust fund whose receipts come from a dedicated levy and whose disbursements are made on a schedule set by law. The sheet notes that the fund is displayed apart from the main budget figures and that Congress has legislated that arrangement.

questions.stem: Under the arrangement described, how should the fund be treated?

options.text: As a second sovereign budget that Congress need not fund each year
options.misconception: treats the trust fund as outside congressional control

options.text: As a statutory exception to the unified budget that Congress has created
As part of the main budget, with no separate display required
options.misconception: ignores the separate display the sheet describes

options.text: As money that the President may spend without any appropriation
options.misconception: confuses a dedicated fund with open spending power

questions.explanation: The sheet describes an off-budget trust fund created by statute, the recognised exception to the single-budget requirement. Congress still appropriates from it, and it grants no free discretion.
questions.hint: Ask whether Congress created the exception deliberately.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an annual deficit from accumulated debt
questions.stem: The revision group asks a student to explain how the national debt figure differs from the deficit figure for a given year.

answer.exemplar: The deficit is a flow measured over one year, the excess of that year's outlays over its revenues, while the debt is the stock accumulated by adding past deficits and subtracting past surpluses. A year with a large deficit therefore raises the debt, and years of surplus reduce it, so the two figures move together over time but describe different things.

questions.explanation: The deficit is a yearly flow and the debt is a running stock built from past deficits net of surpluses. A deficit year adds to the debt, and a surplus year reduces it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the figure covers one year or many.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of an automatic offset requirement
questions.stem: A revision question asks what reason led Congress to adopt offsets for new mandatory spending.

options.text: To keep new commitments from adding to the deficit without a decision on how to pay
To stop Congress from using tax cuts for purposes it disfavours
options.misconception: frames the offset rule as a restriction on tax policy

options.text: To prevent agencies from obligating funds before an appropriation is made
options.misconception: confuses the offset rule with anti-deficiency limits

options.text: To force the President to justify spending above the budget ceiling
options.misconception: reduces the offset rule to a ceiling-enforcement device

questions.explanation: The offset rule exists so new mandatory commitments do not enlarge the deficit without a decision on how to pay. It is not a restriction on tax policy, an anti-deficiency rule, or a ceiling tool.
questions.hint: Ask what problem the rule is meant to prevent.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute an offsetting amount from baseline figures

stimulus.body: A worksheet sets out a pay-as-you-go calculation. Current spending for a programme is 10 billion a year. A proposal would raise it to 13 billion for the next year and the baseline for the comparison year is 10 billion.

questions.stem: On the figures given, what is the offsetting change the proposal would need?

options.text: 3 billion, because the offset equals the increase over the baseline
13 billion, because the offset must cover the whole amount that will be spent
options.misconception: confuses the baseline with spending after the proposal

options.text: 10 billion, because the baseline already accounts for current programme spending
options.misconception: treats the baseline as covering only the proposed increase

options.text: Nothing, because proposals funded from existing money need no offset
options.misconception: assumes spending already in the baseline is free of the rule

questions.explanation: The offset equals the increase over the baseline, so raising spending from 10 billion to 13 billion requires 3 billion. The baseline is the comparison point, not a subtraction from the total cost.
questions.hint: Ask how much the proposal adds to the baseline.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe what the budget office supplies to members
questions.stem: A revision card describes what the Congressional Budget Office provides to members who want the cost of a policy before voting.

options.text: Legal advice on whether a proposal would survive court review
options.misconception: extends the budget office into legal analysis

options.text: Cost estimates and projections of the budget's future path
Draft legislative language implementing the member's preferred policy
options.misconception: makes the budget office a drafting service

options.text: A recommendation on which committee should hear the proposal
options.misconception: treats the budget office as assigning legislative business

questions.explanation: The office supplies cost estimates and baseline projections of future budget paths, letting members weigh a proposal before voting. It gives no legal advice, drafts no text, and assigns no business.
questions.hint: Ask what product the member actually receives.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an offset requirement is enforced
questions.stem: A prompt for the revision group asks a student to describe how an automatic offset requirement is enforced in practice.

answer.exemplar: The budget office scores the legislation and reports whether the offset requirement is triggered and how large the offset must be, and the bill does not take effect unless each chamber waives the requirement. Because the mechanism is automatic, a member cannot defeat it by pointing to unrelated savings unless the offset is actually included in the bill.

questions.explanation: Scoring is automatic, the requirement binds the bill unless both chambers waive it, and savings elsewhere count only when actually in the measure. Scoring is not discretionary.
questions.hint: Ask whether the requirement has to be argued about.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a yearly surplus on the debt
questions.stem: A student works out that in one year federal receipts exceeded outlays by 60 billion and asks what that year produced.

options.text: A rise in the outstanding debt of 60 billion over the year
options.misconception: treats a surplus as an increase in the debt

options.text: A continuing resolution was triggered for the following year
options.misconception: links a surplus to the continuing resolution mechanism

options.text: An automatic sequestration of discretionary programmes
options.misconception: claims a surplus triggers sequestration

options.text: A surplus that reduces the accumulated debt rather than adding to it

questions.explanation: When receipts exceed outlays, the year's surplus reduces the accumulated debt, whereas a deficit would add to it. A surplus has no automatic link to continuing resolutions or to sequestration.
questions.hint: Ask what the surplus does to the stock of debt.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify which accounts absorb an automatic reduction

stimulus.body: A revision note describes how an automatic sequestration is carried out. The amount of the reduction is divided equally between defence and non-defence discretionary accounts, and programmes for veterans, students, and certain other groups are exempt from the reduction.

questions.stem: According to the note, which accounts absorb the cuts?

options.text: Discretionary accounts in defence and non-defence areas, in equal shares
Only non-defence discretionary accounts, since defence spending is untouchable
options.misconception: treats defence accounts as exempt from sequestration

options.text: Mandatory benefit programmes, because those make up most federal spending
options.misconception: picks the wrong category for across-the-board cuts

options.text: Trust fund accounts, which draw on dedicated revenue streams
options.misconception: assumes trust fund balances absorb sequestration

questions.explanation: The note describes an equal split of the reduction across discretionary defence and non-defence accounts, with exempt programmes untouched. Defence spending is not exempt, and trust funds are not hit.
questions.hint: Ask which two categories share the burden.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a continuing resolution cannot fund
questions.stem: A revision prompt asks what a continuing resolution can and cannot do for a programme that has just been authorised.

options.text: It can fund the new programme at the level the President requested
options.misconception: treats a continuing resolution as funding for new programmes

options.text: It can fund the new programme for the full year at its authorised level
options.misconception: gives the instrument the force of an appropriation

options.text: It generally cannot fund the new programme, because no funds have been provided
It must fund the new programme at the authorised level or the programme lapses
options.misconception: makes a continuing resolution a mandate for new spending

questions.explanation: A continuing resolution continues existing funding; it does not supply money for a newly authorised programme with no appropriation behind it. Treating it as a mandate for new spending misstates it.
questions.hint: Ask whether any money was ever provided.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the budget office is described as nonpartisan
questions.stem: Another prompt in the revision set asks a student to explain why the Congressional Budget Office is described in the statutes that created it as nonpartisan.

answer.exemplar: The office exists to give Congress impartial estimates of the cost of proposals, and its institutional insulation from political direction is what allows members of both parties to use its numbers in a debate. The answer should describe the absence of partisan control over the work rather than claiming that every forecast turns out correct.

questions.explanation: Nonpartisanship exists so that members of both parties can rely on the same estimates in debate. The answer should describe the absence of partisan control rather than claim every forecast is correct.
questions.hint: Ask what members need the estimates for.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how current law shapes a baseline
questions.stem: A second question for the revision group: what a baseline holds fixed, and what happens when current law already changes next year.

options.text: A baseline fixes next year's spending as a budget ceiling
options.misconception: treats the baseline as a spending ceiling

options.text: A baseline holds current law in place, so scheduled changes count as policy
A baseline sets the funding level at the lowest of the last three years
options.misconception: invents a three-year averaging rule for the baseline

options.text: A baseline holds the prior year's appropriation fixed for the whole decade
options.misconception: extends the baseline far beyond the comparison year

questions.explanation: A baseline projects current law forward, so a scheduled increase current law requires counts as a policy change and adds to the cost. It is not a ceiling, an average, or a long freeze.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison assumes about enacted law.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a congressional disapproval is recorded
questions.stem: A revision question asks in what form a congressional response to a proposed rescission is recorded.

options.text: Either house may pass a resolution of disapproval, which blocks the rescission
Both houses must pass a resolution, or the rescission takes effect
options.misconception: turns disapproval into a positive approval rule

options.text: The President may overrule a disapproval by signing the rescission
options.misconception: invents a presidential override of the disapproval

options.text: The rescission takes effect unless a committee votes to block it
options.misconception: puts the decision with a committee, not a chamber

questions.explanation: The statute works by disapproval, so either house can block the rescission and the President cannot make it effective alone. Positive approval in both houses would invert it.
questions.hint: Ask how many houses are needed to block it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the status of a member's request for a score

stimulus.body: A revision summary notes that members of Congress may ask the Congressional Budget Office for an estimate of a proposal, and that the office decides for itself whether and how to prepare it, subject to the instructions Congress gives by statute. The summary adds that the office does not take direction from any individual member.

questions.stem: Under the summary, what is the status of a member's request for an estimate?

options.text: It must be answered within a fixed period set by the chamber rules
options.misconception: invents a mandatory response deadline for score requests

options.text: It is granted only if the request is endorsed by the committee chair
options.misconception: makes score requests depend on committee leadership

options.text: It is answered only if the member's own office drafts the scoring request
options.misconception: shifts the work of scoring onto the requesting member

options.text: It is a request the office may accept or decline, within the statute's terms

questions.explanation: The office takes direction through statute rather than from members, so a request is a request. No fixed deadline, chair approval, or member drafting is part of the arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the office must say yes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the figures needed to compute a deficit
questions.stem: Another revision question asks which pair of figures is needed to work out a year's deficit.

options.text: The debt ceiling and the level of the outstanding debt
options.misconception: uses the debt figures to compute a yearly shortfall

options.text: The previous year's deficit and the change in the debt
options.misconception: confuses the deficit with the change in outstanding debt

options.text: The year's outlays and the year's revenues
The baseline and the enacted appropriation for the year
options.misconception: borrows the pay-as-you-go comparison pair

questions.explanation: The deficit is computed from the year's outlays less the year's revenues, which is why they appear in the same table. The debt level and the baseline play no part in the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Ask which two figures cover the same twelve months.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The unified budget and off-budget items
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the unified budget requirement
questions.stem: Another prompt for the revision set asks a student to explain what the requirement that all federal money be presented in a single budget is designed to achieve.

answer.exemplar: A single budget makes the federal government's finances visible as a whole, so Congress must authorise spending and raise revenue in the same document and the public can see the total claim on resources. It also disciplines the use of off-budget trust funds, which exist by statute but remain subject to congressional control.

questions.explanation: A single budget makes the whole of federal spending and taxation visible in one place, which disciplines appropriations. The statutory exceptions to it were created by Congress itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the requirement makes visible.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the President may not substitute targeted cuts
questions.stem: A student asks whether the President may reduce an agency programme instead of applying an across-the-board cut when sequestration is triggered.

options.text: Yes, because the President controls the programme's funding level
options.misconception: confuses programme management with the sequestration method

options.text: No, because the across-the-board reduction is set by statute and must be applied
Yes, so long as the total reduction matches what sequestration requires
options.misconception: allows targeted cuts in place of the formula

options.text: Yes, because the President may request that the cut be rescinded
options.misconception: invents a rescission option inside the sequestration process

questions.explanation: Because the reduction is specified by statute, the President must apply the across-the-board method rather than substitute his own plan. Rescission is a separate process.
questions.hint: Ask whether the method is fixed in advance.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what counts toward an offset

stimulus.body: A revision note states that a bill increasing direct spending or reducing receipts triggers the offset requirement, and that spending for a new programme with an initial cost is measured against the baseline for its first full year of operation. The note adds that tax increases and spending cuts count toward the offset.

questions.stem: According to the note, what counts toward satisfying the requirement?

options.text: Offsetting revenue increases and spending reductions included in the bill
Any savings the executive expects to find during the coming year
options.misconception: counts executive-expected savings toward a statutory offset

options.text: Only spending reductions, because revenue measures cannot offset a new programme
options.misconception: denies that revenue increases count toward the offset

options.text: Whatever the sponsor's own budget resolution promises to save
options.misconception: treats a resolution promise as satisfying the statutory test

questions.explanation: The note describes an offset met by revenue increases and spending reductions carried in the bill, so promised savings that are not enacted do not count. Revenue measures are part of the offset.
questions.hint: Ask whether the savings must actually be in the bill.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why analysts may reach different conclusions
questions.stem: A revision question asks why two analysts using the same budget office figures reach different conclusions.

options.text: Because one of them used a different baseline year entirely
options.misconception: blames a baseline year difference where none exists

options.text: Because the figures the office publishes are revised after each score
options.misconception: assumes the underlying score changes between analysts

options.text: Because they may be measuring the proposal against different reference points
Because only the committee majority may use the published estimates
options.misconception: invents a rule restricting use of public scores

questions.explanation: The published figures are the same for both analysts, so any difference comes from the comparison each chooses, such as a different baseline or year. Restricting estimates would not explain it.
questions.hint: Ask what each analyst chose to compare against.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the budget office publishes multi-year projections
questions.stem: One question for the revision set asks a student to explain why the Congressional Budget Office publishes multi-year projections rather than a single figure.

answer.exemplar: Multi-year projections show how spending and revenues develop under current law once scheduled changes and interest costs are taken into account, so members can see the trajectory a decision produces rather than only its first-year effect. The projections are not forecasts of what any administration will choose to do, and they are conditional on the law as it stands.

questions.explanation: The projections describe how the budget develops under current law, so members see the long-run cost of a decision rather than its first year. They are not predictions of future policy choices.
questions.hint: Ask what the projection follows rather than predicts.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a missing chamber waiver

stimulus.body: A handout explains that a proposal which fails the automatic offset test can still become law if the requirement is waived. It states that the waiver must be recorded separately for the House and for the Senate, and that a waiver passed by one chamber does not bind the other.

questions.stem: Under the handout, what follows for a proposal that lacks a waiver from one chamber?

options.text: It cannot take effect unless the other chamber also grants the waiver
It takes effect because the waiver requirement has been satisfied in part
options.misconception: treats a partial waiver as satisfying the requirement

options.text: It must be sent back for rescoring before the chambers vote again
options.misconception: invents a rescoring step between the chambers

options.text: It takes effect if the President declines to veto the bill
options.misconception: makes presidential inaction a substitute for the waiver

questions.explanation: Each chamber must grant its own waiver, so a proposal lacking one from a single chamber cannot take effect. Partial satisfaction and presidential inaction are irrelevant to the requirement.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if one chamber declines.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish debt held by the public from total debt
questions.stem: Another revision question asks how debt held by the public differs from total federal debt.

options.text: It is larger, because it includes money held in federal accounts
options.misconception: adds intragovernmental holdings instead of removing them

options.text: It is identical, because the two figures are set by statute to match
options.misconception: assumes the two debt measures are required to be the same

options.text: It is smaller, because it excludes the obligations of state governments
options.misconception: treats the difference as arising from state borrowing

options.text: It is smaller, because intragovernmental holdings are subtracted from the total

questions.explanation: Debt held by the public excludes the government's own holdings in federal accounts, so it is smaller than total federal debt. It has nothing to do with state borrowing, and the figures need not match.
questions.hint: Ask which holdings are counted as inside government.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a continuing resolution avoids disruption
questions.stem: A prompt for revision asks a student to explain how a continuing resolution is designed to avoid a disruption in government operations.

answer.exemplar: A continuing resolution continues existing appropriations at their prior rate and conditions for a short period, so agencies keep operating while the appropriations process runs its course, and any new programme with no money behind it simply waits. It is a temporary bridge rather than a way to govern for a year, and it does not authorise anything Congress has not already provided.

questions.explanation: A continuing resolution preserves existing operations at prior rates while the ordinary appropriations process continues. It neither funds new commitments nor substitutes for an annual appropriation.
questions.hint: Ask what the instrument preserves and for how long.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify exemptions and the fallback after a cut
questions.stem: The revision sheet asks about exemptions: which spending is exempt from an automatic cut, and what happens if the cut is found to be insufficient.

options.text: Mandatory spending is exempt, and the President may then impose a further cut
options.misconception: invents a presidential power to add cuts after sequestration

options.text: Interest is exempt, and Congress must then enact a replacement plan
options.misconception: makes a replacement statute the remedy for an inadequate cut

options.text: Mandatory spending and interest are exempt, and the shortfall triggers a new process
Nothing is exempt, and a shortfall must be cured by the President alone
options.misconception: denies the statutory exemptions entirely

questions.explanation: Mandatory programmes and interest on the debt are protected from the automatic reduction. If the cut is judged insufficient, the statute sets out a further process, not presidential discretion.
questions.hint: Ask what the statute provides if the cut falls short.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify which executive action is a deferral
questions.stem: A revision card asks which of two executive actions falls within the congressional disapproval process.

options.text: Postponing the start of a programme Congress has already authorised
options.misconception: confuses delayed authority with deferred funds

options.text: Postponing the spending of money Congress has already appropriated
Reducing the staff complement of a federal field office
options.misconception: treats personnel reductions as deferrals of funds

options.text: Delaying a rulemaking that Congress directed an agency to complete
options.misconception: treats agency scheduling choices as appropriations decisions

questions.explanation: A deferral of appropriated money is within the disapproval process, so postponing the spending of funds cannot proceed unilaterally. Delaying new authority or trimming staff are different matters.
questions.hint: Ask whether funds already granted are involved.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features that make an instrument a continuing resolution

stimulus.body: A revision handout reproduces the shape of a short-term funding law. It states the period it covers, directs each agency to continue spending at the rate and under the conditions of the prior period, and is set to end on a stated date unless replaced by a regular appropriation.

questions.stem: Under the handout's description, what makes the measure a continuing resolution rather than an annual appropriation?

options.text: It continues existing spending briefly and sets a date on which it ends
It is enacted in the middle of the year rather than at its start
options.misconception: ties the instrument to the calendar rather than its content

options.text: It covers the same programmes as the previous year's appropriation
options.misconception: identifies the instrument by its subject matter

options.text: It is approved by both houses without any presidential signature
options.misconception: invents a signature rule for the instrument

questions.explanation: The handout shows the features that matter: a short continuation of existing spending and a stated end date. When it runs out, the money it carried lapses unless a regular appropriation replaces it.
questions.hint: Ask about the duration and the end date.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a baseline from an appropriation
questions.stem: A student asks why the word baseline appears in budget debates when it does not mean the same thing as an appropriation.

options.text: Because a baseline is the amount an agency says it needs to operate
options.misconception: treats the baseline as an agency's request

options.text: Because a baseline is the funding level for the coming year as proposed
options.misconception: confuses the baseline with a funding proposal

options.text: Because a baseline is fixed by the congressional budget resolution
options.misconception: ties the baseline to a resolution rather than to law

options.text: Because a baseline is a comparison point built from existing law

questions.explanation: A baseline is a comparison point constructed from existing law, used to measure what a proposal would change. It is not an agency's request, a funding proposal, or a figure from a resolution.
questions.hint: Ask what the baseline is built from.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how interest payments relate to deficit and debt
questions.stem: A further prompt asks a student to explain how interest payments on the debt fit into the relationship between the deficit, the debt, and the budget.

answer.exemplar: Interest is an outlay, so it enters the current year's budget and, if receipts are lower than outlays, it contributes to that year's deficit and to the growth of the accumulated debt. Because interest on the public debt is not a discretionary programme, it is not reduced by an across-the-board sequestration, which means it can crowd out spending that could otherwise be cut.

questions.explanation: Interest sits on the outlay side of the budget, so it contributes to deficits and to debt growth. Because it is protected from automatic cuts, it becomes a fixed claim on later budgets.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the budget interest sits on.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an announcement cannot defer appropriated funds

stimulus.body: A study group asks what the legal position is where an agency head announces in a press conference that a programme will be delayed. A lawmaker asks whether the announcement itself changes what the agency may spend.

questions.stem: What is the legal position on the facts described?

options.text: The programme is delayed, because the executive controls agency operations
options.misconception: treats an executive announcement as self-executing

options.text: The announcement alone does not change the agency's spending authority
The announcement is valid if the agency head is acting under an executive order
options.misconception: believes an executive order supplies a congressional cure

options.text: The announcement is valid once the agency publishes it in the Federal Register
options.misconception: treats publication as the missing legal step

questions.explanation: An announcement is not a legal instrument, so it cannot defer or cancel appropriated money; a deferral must follow the disapproval process. An executive order does not supply that step.
questions.hint: Ask whether a press statement has legal force.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a continuing resolution interacts with the new year
questions.stem: A revision question asks about a continuing resolution still in force as the new fiscal year begins.

options.text: The prior-year rate continues, since the resolution speaks to the year ahead
options.misconception: assumes the resolution always spans the new year

options.text: Spending stops at midnight, because the resolution expires with the year
options.misconception: assumes a lapse whenever the new year begins

options.text: Funding continues only as long as the resolution runs, and then the question returns
The President must propose a new continuing resolution for the year
options.misconception: makes the continuing resolution a presidential instrument

questions.explanation: A continuing resolution operates for the period it states, so it may or may not reach into the new fiscal year. When it ends, the funding question returns to the ordinary process.
questions.hint: Ask how long the instrument lasts.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The unified budget and off-budget items
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish off-budget display from exemption
questions.stem: A further question asks a student to explain the difference between a fund displayed outside the main budget figures and a fund exempt from congressional appropriations.

answer.exemplar: A display outside the main budget changes how the programme is presented, not whether Congress must authorise its spending; money still moves on an appropriation, and Congress still examines it in a separate statement of the federal finances. Exemption from appropriations is a different and stronger thing, and it too rests on a statute rather than on administrative practice.

questions.explanation: Off-budget display changes presentation, not legal authority, and money still moves on an appropriation. Exemption from appropriations is a stronger arrangement, and it too rests on statute.
questions.hint: Ask whether presentation and authority are the same.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify which legislation the offset rule targets
questions.stem: A further revision question asks which kind of legislation the automatic offset requirement is aimed at.

options.text: Legislation that creates a new mandatory spending commitment
Any bill that increases federal spending in the current year
options.misconception: extends the offset rule to all current-year spending

options.text: Every bill that reduces revenue, including a change in tax rates
options.misconception: makes the rule apply to all revenue measures without limit

options.text: All bills reported by a committee with budget-related jurisdiction
options.misconception: ties the trigger to committee jurisdiction

questions.explanation: The requirement targets measures that create mandatory commitments or reduce receipts on a continuing basis, since those enlarge future deficits. It does not reach every spending or revenue change.
questions.hint: Ask which measures enlarge future deficits.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a proposal's score is computed
questions.stem: Two further points for revision: what a baseline measures, and how a proposal's score is computed against it.

options.text: A baseline measures next year's expected outlays, and the score is the difference
options.misconception: treats the score as a simple subtraction from a forecast

options.text: A baseline measures the ceiling on discretionary spending, and the score is the excess
options.misconception: treats the baseline as a discretionary spending cap

options.text: A baseline measures this year's enacted appropriation, and the score is the increase
options.misconception: uses enacted appropriations as the comparison point

options.text: A baseline measures current law in the comparison year, and the score is the difference

questions.explanation: A baseline projects current law into the comparison year, and the score is the difference between the proposal's cost and that baseline. A forecast or a discretionary cap is not it.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison line is built from.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the distinctive products of the budget office
questions.stem: A revision card lists what the Congressional Budget Office does that some other congressional offices do not.

options.text: It prepares the legislative text of appropriations measures
options.misconception: credits the budget office with drafting appropriations text

options.text: It publishes the budget projections and scores used to weigh proposals
It advises members on the merits of a policy proposal
options.misconception: turns a scoring function into policy advocacy

options.text: It conducts the oversight hearings that examine programme performance
options.misconception: assigns the budget office the hearing function of committees

questions.explanation: The distinctive products are the published projections and the scoring of proposals, which give members a common basis for weighing costs. Drafting, advocacy, and hearings belong elsewhere.
questions.hint: Ask what the office publishes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the statutory trigger for automatic reductions

stimulus.body: A revision card lists three figures: a statutory limit on the deficit for the coming year, a limit on total borrowing, and a spending cap for discretionary programmes. It asks students to identify which of the three is the trigger for automatic across-the-board reductions.

questions.stem: According to the card, which figure triggers automatic reductions?

options.text: The limit on total borrowing, because borrowing measures the deficit indirectly
options.misconception: picks the debt ceiling rather than the deficit trigger

options.text: The spending cap for discretionary programmes, because it is measured annually
options.misconception: confuses the discretionary cap with the deficit trigger

options.text: The statutory limit on the deficit, because the cuts follow from reaching it
All three, because each of them separately compels the same result
options.misconception: treats the three figures as interchangeable triggers

questions.explanation: The automatic reduction follows from reaching the statutory limit on the deficit, and the other two figures belong to separate mechanisms. Treating them as interchangeable misidentifies the trigger.
questions.hint: Ask which figure the statute ties to the cuts.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain when the offsetting change must operate
questions.stem: A revision question asks when the offsetting change accompanying new mandatory spending must operate.

options.text: At the same time as the new commitment it pays for
In the following fiscal year, since the first year may be absorbed
options.misconception: allows a one-year deferral of the offsetting change

options.text: Whenever the agency concerned determines it can absorb the cost
options.misconception: leaves the timing of the offset to the spending agency

options.text: Only if the offset does not reduce spending below the statutory floor
options.misconception: invents a floor-based condition on the offset

questions.explanation: The offset operates at the same time as the spending it supports, so a later saving does not satisfy the requirement. Neither agency discretion nor a floor for offset savings appears in it.
questions.hint: Ask when the saving has to happen.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why repeated deficits raise the debt
questions.stem: A study question asks a student to explain why persistent deficits raise the debt rather than simply increasing spending capacity.

answer.exemplar: A deficit means the government has spent more than it collected in a year, so the shortfall must be financed by borrowing, and borrowing accumulates rather than disappears. Over a run of deficit years the outstanding obligations of the federal government grow, and the interest on that larger balance becomes a claim on future budgets, which is what makes the effect cumulative rather than annual.

questions.explanation: Each deficit must be financed by borrowing, so the balances accumulate over time. The interest on the growing balance then becomes a recurring claim on future budgets.
questions.hint: Ask how a deficit is paid for in the first place.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the source of congressional power over rescissions
questions.stem: A revision prompt asks which source gives Congress authority over a proposed rescission.

options.text: The appropriations clause alone, without any implementing statute
options.misconception: ignores the need for the implementing statute

options.text: The rule that members may introduce disapproval resolutions
options.misconception: relies on chamber rules rather than statute

options.text: The President's duty to submit an annual budget to Congress
options.misconception: derives the blocking power from the budget submission duty

options.text: A statute requiring congressional approval of any rescission proposal

questions.explanation: The authority comes from the statute requiring proposed rescissions and deferrals to be submitted and giving Congress power to disapprove them. The appropriations clause alone does not do this.
questions.hint: Ask which legal instrument creates the procedure.

questions.topic: The unified budget and off-budget items
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a single budget document must contain

stimulus.body: A revision handout describes the budget submission. The President submits estimates of receipts and expenditures for the coming year, the budget is presented as a single document covering all federal programmes, and the funds displayed outside the main figures still require appropriations before they may be spent.

questions.stem: Under the handout's framing, what does the single-document presentation imply?

options.misconception: treats separate display as freedom to spend

options.text: All federal spending is presented and voted on as one budget
Only programmes with outlays above a threshold appear in the document
options.misconception: invents a threshold for inclusion in the budget

options.text: The President may submit only the programmes he intends to fund
options.misconception: invents a presidential power to omit programmes

questions.explanation: The handout describes the budget as a single document in which all federal programmes appear, with separate funds still subject to appropriation. Thresholds and presidential omissions play no part.
questions.hint: Ask what the single document must contain.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a limit on the budget office's role
questions.stem: A revision card states a limit on the budget office's role that students often get wrong.

options.text: It may not publish any estimate of a bill before the vote
options.misconception: invents a prohibition on pre-vote estimates

options.text: It may not work for committees of either chamber
options.misconception: makes the office unavailable to committees

options.text: It may not recommend which option a member should support
It may not score a proposal that would increase mandatory spending
options.misconception: invents a ban on scoring mandatory proposals

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the baseline is built from current law
questions.stem: Another study question asks a student to explain why the baseline used for scoring is built from law already in force rather than from the budget the President proposes.

answer.exemplar: The baseline is a neutral measuring stick. If it were built from the President's budget, any proposal would be scored against the administration's own choices and would always look like a modest change, whereas projecting current law shows what happens if the legislature does nothing, so the cost of acting can be compared with the cost of not acting.

questions.explanation: A baseline built from existing law is a neutral comparison point. One drawn from a budget proposal would measure everything against a partisan starting line and hide the cost of inaction.
questions.hint: Ask why the comparison line must not favour a side.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify which accounts are subject to sequestration
questions.stem: A fourth revision question asks which part of the budget an automatic sequestration actually reduces.

options.text: Discretionary programme authority, leaving mandatory commitments intact
Mandatory benefit programmes, because they represent most federal spending
options.misconception: picks mandatory programmes as the target

options.text: Trust fund balances held for future social insurance payments
